Sample.evidence_source: We recruited a total of 36 young men into the study.

Country.evidence_source: The study received full Office of Research Ethics Committee, Northern Ireland, approval.

Population.evidence_source: A core criterion for involvement was that participants had been actively suicidal at some time in their lives, ascertained through use of the Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation–Worst. This is a well-validated tool for assessing suicidal intent at its worst, irrespective of time elapsed (Beck, Brown, & Steer, 1997; Beck, Brown, Steer, Dahlsgaard, & Grisham, 1999). All participants scored as having significant suicidal ideation, with 85% scoring as having severe to profound suicidal ideation.

Type.evidence_source: The need to allow participants the opportunity to express in personally meaningful ways the circumstances of their suicidal behavior prompted our use of in-depth interviews as the means of data collection. All interviews were audio-recorded, with permission.

Area.evidence_source: Participants' access to formal and/or informal (mental) health services as well as their understanding of the factors that helped maintain their wish to stay alive were explored.2 Interviews began with an opening exploratory question that asked something like, "Could we just start by telling me about your experiences around the time you felt suicidal?" This question was designed to open up the interview so that, from the outset, it took the form of a discussion between interviewer and participant. Thereafter, a series of open-ended questions enabled a young man to continue to talk about his experiences in terms of what he considered to be meaningful to his own suicidality.
